correctness.rationale: The exponential Hermite generating function gives the even series (1+u)^(-1/2) exp(ux²/[2(1+u)]); this also follows from the explicit Hermite coefficients of x^(2k). The diagonal Mehler series at x/sqrt(2) has the same exponential and prefactor (1-u²)^(-1/2). Multiply it with u=gamma*t by sqrt(1-gamma*t)/(1-t) and extract t^m. This verifies the coefficient identity formally, with no restriction on gamma, including m=0. The representation has nonnegative weights on [0,1]; outside this interval the identity is a linear combination of squares, not a positivity certificate. All nonconstant coefficients of a_m as a polynomial in gamma are negative, so a_m(gamma)>=a_m(1)=[t^m](1-t)^(-1/2)=binom(2m,m)/4^m. Negative gamma fails with m=1 and large |x|. At x=0 and gamma>1, divide by (-gamma)^m c_m with c_m=binom(2m,m)/4^m. Each fixed reverse-index ratio c_(m-r)/c_m tends to 1; for r<=m/2 the ratio is uniformly bounded, and for r>m/2 the omitted sum is O(sqrt(m)*gamma^(-m/2)). The limit gamma/(1+gamma)>0 gives a genuinely negative value for all sufficiently large odd m. Equation (2.11) of the quadrature paper has this partial sum and strictly positive other factors: the classical Gaussian weights, normalization and exponential. The usual scale has finite length ell>0 and 0<gamma<1. This establishes only the Mercer-truncated approximate weights. Independently ran `python audit_checks/independent_replays.py 1`: exact coefficient comparisons of the formal Hermite/Mehler product through degree 24 in u, the central-binomial bounds, and exact negative witness m=393 at gamma=101/100. This is a finite corroboration, not the proof; submitted code was inspected, not executed.

value.rationale: A positivity certificate for weights in a specified practical quadrature approximation resolves a motivated sign question that node sampling cannot settle. The same identity gives a uniform-in-x lower bound and a sharp all-degree real parameter classification with explicit qualitatively different obstruction on each side. It does not promise conditioning improvements, exact-kernel weights, or error rates.
